findings.who: A landlord whose unit has had a long-term tenant since spring 2025. They paid for listings in January and February 2025 to fill a vacancy.
findings.why_no: The gate is the bare noun 'Advertising' with no verb or year. A filer reads it as 'is this property advertised?' in the present tense and answers no because the unit is rented now.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses ...'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you (or your spouse, or anyone acting for you) pay for advertising or listings to find renters for this property at any time in 2025, even if it is rented now?'

findings.who: A short-term or long-term landlord who paid listing fees to an online rental site, printed 'For Rent' signs or flyers, or paid a featured-listing upgrade. They never bought anything they would call 'advertising'.
findings.why_no: The single word 'Advertising' suggests paid ads such as newspaper or media. Listing fees, signs and platform promotion are not perceived as advertising.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents' commissions ...'
findings.fix: Add help text: 'Includes online listing fees, featured-listing upgrades, signs, flyers and classified ads used to find renters.'

findings.who: An owner whose property manager advertised the vacancy and deducted the cost from the rent it remitted. The year-end owner statement shows the advertising charge.
findings.why_no: The owner never paid for advertising personally or with their own card, so they answer no. The gated question says 'paid in 2025', which reinforces that reading.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column.'
findings.fix: Ask whether advertising was paid by you or by a property manager or agent on your behalf, including amounts withheld from rents. Check the manager's year-end statement.

findings.who: Spouses filing jointly who co-own the rental, where the spouse handled and paid for the vacancy ads from their own account.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks for 'your share'. On a joint return the filer may treat the spouse's payments as not theirs and answer no at the gate.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property ...'
findings.fix: Word the gate as 'Did you or your spouse pay ...'. On a joint return, define 'your share' as the combined share of both spouses.

findings.who: An accrual-basis landlord who incurred advertising in December 2025 and paid the invoice in January 2026.
findings.why_no: The gated question says 'paid in 2025', so the filer answers no or enters zero. The instructions allow expenses paid or incurred under the filer's method.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses ...'
findings.fix: Say 'paid in 2025 (or incurred in 2025, if you use the accrual method)'.

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A short-term or vacation rental host whose platform charges each guest a cleaning fee. The host pays a cleaner out of that fee, and the gross rents reported to the host include the fee.
findings.why_no: The bare label 'Cleaning and maintenance' gives no guidance. The host thinks the guest paid for cleaning, not the host, so there was no cleaning expense of their own.
findings.irs_text: "You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees..." (i1040se 2025 p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21)
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you, your spouse, a co-owner, or anyone acting for you (such as a property manager or rental platform) pay for cleaning, janitorial, lawn, pest control, pool, snow removal or similar upkeep of this property in 2025? Include cleaning paid from guest cleaning fees that are counted in your rents.'

findings.who: An owner whose property manager pays cleaners and maintenance vendors out of collected rents. The owner receives only a monthly owner statement and a net payout.
findings.why_no: The owner never wrote a check for cleaning and remembers only the management fee. The statement may lump vendor payments together, so the owner answers no.
findings.irs_text: "Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column. You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses..." (i1040se 2025 p. 6)
findings.fix: In the gate help, say that amounts a manager or agent paid from your rents count, and tell the filer to check the owner statement's expense detail.

findings.who: A filer who rents out a room, a basement unit, or one side of a duplex they live in. They pay for cleaning or upkeep of common areas, or of the whole building.
findings.why_no: Read 'For this rental property', the filer counts only cleaning of the rented part itself. Whole-house or common-area cleaning seems personal or not 'for the rental', even though the helper takes the amount before any division for personal use.
findings.irs_text: "If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part." (i1040se 2025 p. 6)
findings.fix: Add: 'Include cleaning and upkeep of the whole building or shared areas; the tool will divide it between rental and personal use.'

findings.who: A landlord whose only upkeep costs are lawn care, landscaping, pest control, pool service, gutter cleaning or snow removal.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'cleaning' literally as housecleaning, and does not see yard or pest service as 'maintenance' as distinct from repairs.
findings.irs_text: "You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses..." (i1040se 2025 p. 6)
findings.fix: List examples in the gate (janitorial, turnover cleaning, lawn and landscaping, pest control, pool, snow removal, gutter cleaning). Point to Other expenses for anything else.

findings.who: A landlord who cleans the unit personally and buys only cleaning supplies and equipment rentals, such as a carpet shampooer.
findings.why_no: The filer reasons that they did the cleaning themselves, and the instructions say not to deduct the value of their own labor. They answer no and drop the supplies and equipment cost, unless the tool clearly sends those to Supplies.
findings.irs_text: "Do not deduct the value of your own labor" (i1040se 2025 p. 6), which excludes only the labor, not out-of-pocket costs.
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'If you did the work yourself, your time is not deductible, but supplies and equipment you paid for are (enter them here or under Supplies).'

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly who own a rental together, where the spouse paid the cleaner from a separate account.
findings.why_no: The gated question says 'paid in 2025 (your share)'. The answering spouse may report only their own half or their own payments, or answer the gate no because they personally paid nothing.
findings.irs_text: "Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column." (i1040se 2025 p. 6)
findings.fix: Say 'paid by you or your spouse (on a joint return, include both spouses' shares)'.

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A landlord paid a leasing agent a commission in 2023 or 2024 to secure a multi-year lease that is still running in 2025. Commissions paid to obtain a lease are amortized over the lease term (Pub. 527), so part of that commission is deductible in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks for commissions 'paid in 2025', and the bare gate 'Commissions' reads as this year's payments. The filer paid no commission in 2025 and truthfully answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... management fees, agents' commissions, and depreciation.' The text sets no paid-this-year limit; Pub. 527 requires lease commissions to be amortized over the lease term.
findings.fix: Gate: 'For this rental property, did you or your spouse pay any commission in 2025, or in an earlier year for a lease that is still running in 2025 (for example, to an agent who found a renter)?' Add a follow-up that computes this year's amortized share of earlier-year lease commissions.

findings.who: A landlord whose property manager or rental platform (for example a short-term rental host-fee platform, or a leasing agent) keeps its commission out of the rent and remits only the net amount.
findings.why_no: The filer never wrote a check for a commission and sees only net deposits, so 'Commissions paid' looks inapplicable. They may also file the agent's tenant-placement fee under 'management fees' and not think of it as a commission.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents' commissions, and depreciation.'
findings.fix: Help text: 'Include commissions or fees an agent, manager, or platform kept out of your rent before paying you (report the gross rent as income). Include fees for finding or placing a tenant even if your manager calls them part of its fee.'

findings.who: An accrual-basis owner of a rental property who owed an agent's commission for a lease signed in late 2025 but paid it in January 2026.
findings.why_no: The word 'paid' in 'Commissions paid ... in 2025' leads the filer to answer no, because the cash left in 2026.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... agents' commissions ...'
findings.fix: Use 'paid or incurred (if you use the accrual method)', or ask the filer's accounting method first.

findings.who: Spouses who file jointly and co-own a rental property, where only the spouse paid the leasing agent.
findings.why_no: The gated question says 'your share', and the gate does not mention a spouse, so the filer may count only commissions they paid personally.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column.'
findings.fix: Use 'you or your spouse' in the gate, and say 'your share (on a joint return, include your spouse's share)'.

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A landlord who paid a three-year landlord policy in full in 2023 or 2024, and that policy covers all of 2025. They paid nothing for insurance in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate says only 'Insurance' and gives no time frame or help. Filers read a yearly expense question as 'did you pay insurance this year', so a filer who wrote no insurance check in 2025 answers no.
findings.irs_text: p527 (2025) p. 5: 'If you pay an insurance premium for more than 1 year in advance, you can't deduct the total premium in the year you pay it. For each year of coverage, you can deduct only the part of the premium payment that applies to that year.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was this property insured for any part of 2025, including by a policy paid in an earlier year that covers more than one year, or by your lender from escrow?'

findings.who: A landlord whose mortgage servicer pays the hazard or flood premium from an escrow account funded by the monthly mortgage payment. The filer never sees an insurance bill.
findings.why_no: They think of the payment as 'the mortgage' and the insurance as something the lender handles, so they answer no to 'Insurance'.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, ...'
findings.fix: Add help to the gate: 'Include insurance paid by your lender from an escrow account (see Form 1098, box for escrow or your annual escrow statement).'

findings.who: A filer who rents out one unit of a duplex they live in, or rooms in their home, under one homeowner's policy on the whole building.
findings.why_no: The question says 'For this rental property', and the policy is the filer's homeowner's insurance on their home, not a landlord policy on 'the rental'. So they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6: 'Renting out part of your home. If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part.'
findings.fix: Add help to the gate: 'Include a homeowner's or other policy that covers the rented part along with your own home. The share for the rented part is figured later.'

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where the spouse who manages the rental paid the premium from a separate account, and the other spouse is the one completing the return.
findings.why_no: The gated question speaks of 'your share', and the filer reads 'you' as themselves alone. They know of no insurance they paid, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property ... such as ... insurance'
findings.fix: Word the gate: 'Did you or your spouse have insurance on this property for 2025 (paid by either of you)?'

findings.who: A landlord whose only coverage on the property is a separate flood, earthquake, liability or umbrella, or rent-loss policy, or private mortgage insurance on the rental loan. There is no standard landlord or hazard policy.
findings.why_no: They read 'Insurance' as the ordinary property policy and do not count specialty or liability coverage, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... insurance'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Any insurance for this property: fire, theft, flood, earthquake, liability, rent loss, or the rental's share of an umbrella policy (vehicle insurance goes under auto expenses).'

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21
p. 5, Insurance premiums paid in advance, "For each year of coverage, you can deduct only the part of the premium payment that applies to that year"

findings.who: A landlord whose only professional cost for the property was the part of their CPA or paid preparer's bill for preparing Schedule E, or for tax advice on the rental. They hired no lawyer.
findings.why_no: The gate shows only the bare label 'Legal and other professional fees'. They read it as attorney costs. The mention of tax preparation appears only in the gated question, which they never see after answering no. They also treat the tax-prep bill as a personal cost for the whole return, not a cost of 'this rental property'.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Line 10: 'Include on line 10 fees for tax advice and the preparation of tax forms related to your rental real estate or royalty properties.'
findings.fix: Put the examples in the gate: 'For this rental property, did you pay any legal, accounting, bookkeeping, tax advice, or tax preparation fees (including the part of your return-preparation fee for this property)?'

findings.who: A filer whose Schedule E column is a royalty property, such as an oil or gas interest, a copyright, a patent, or NIL royalties. They paid an accountant or a lawyer for licensing or tax work on it.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'For this rental property'. A royalty owner may decide the question does not apply, because they have no rental property, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Line 10: 'fees for tax advice and the preparation of tax forms related to your rental real estate or royalty properties.'
findings.fix: Say 'For this rental or royalty property' in the gate. Or, when the column is a royalty property, swap in property-type-specific wording.

findings.who: A landlord who uses a property manager. The manager paid the eviction attorney, accountant, or bookkeeper out of the rents and listed those costs only as deductions on the monthly owner statement.
findings.why_no: The filer never paid a professional directly. They think of all deductions on the statement as 'management fees', so they answer no to legal and professional fees.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Line 10: 'Include on line 10 fees for tax advice and the preparation of tax forms...'; General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... management fees, agents' commissions'
findings.fix: Add help to the gate: 'Include fees a property manager paid for you out of rents (shown on your owner statement).'

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse handled a jointly owned rental and paid its accountant and legal fees from a separate account.
findings.why_no: The gate has no subject, and the gated question says 'your share'. The answering filer knows of no fees they paid themselves, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column.'
findings.fix: Word the gate as 'Did you or your spouse pay ... for this property?'

locators: p. 6, Line 10

findings.who: A filer whose rental shows a small profit on line 21 this year but has losses disallowed under the at-risk rules in earlier years carried forward on Form 6198. Those losses are financed by a nonrecourse seller loan.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed only from this year's line 21, which is zero or positive, so the at-risk question is never asked. The carried-forward losses, together with this year's figures, are a loss in the activity that is still limited by the at-risk amount.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'In most cases, you must complete Form 6198 to figure your loss if you have: • A loss from an activity ... and • Amounts in the activity for which you are not at risk'; p. 7, Line 21: 'If you have amounts for which you are not at risk, use Form 6198 to determine the amount of your deductible loss'
findings.fix: Gate on a loss in the activity, not only on line 21 < 0. Add the question 'Do you have losses from this property that were not allowed in an earlier year (for example, on Form 6198 or Form 8582)?' Ask the at-risk question if either the current or the carried-forward amount gives a loss.

findings.who: A filer who sold or disposed of a rental property this year at a loss reported on Form 4797. The property was financed by a nonrecourse loan from the seller. Rents less expenses on line 21 are zero or positive.
findings.why_no: The gate looks only at line 21, which excludes the loss on disposition. The disposition loss is part of the activity's loss under the at-risk rules, so the computed condition is false while the at-risk limit applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3, At-Risk Rules: 'The at-risk rules in most cases limit the amount of loss (including loss on the disposition of assets) you can claim to the amount you could actually lose in the activity.'
findings.fix: Make the gate 'line 21 < 0 OR this property was sold or disposed of this year, with a loss on the disposition (Form 4797 or Form 8949)'. Alternatively, ask 'Did you sell, exchange or otherwise dispose of this property, or any part of it, in 2025?' and include the disposition result in the loss test.

findings.who: A filer whose rental is personal property, such as equipment or vehicles, or a mineral or royalty interest reported on Schedule E. It is financed by a nonrecourse loan from a bank.
findings.why_no: The question excepts 'a mortgage on it from a bank, government or other regular lender'. The filer reads the bank loan, or a chattel mortgage, as excepted. Qualified nonrecourse financing applies only to real property, other than mineral property.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'Qualified nonrecourse financing is treated as an amount at risk if it is secured by real property used in an activity of holding real property'; '• Borrowed by you in connection with the activity of holding real property (other than mineral property)'
findings.fix: Limit the exception explicitly: 'other than a mortgage on a building or land (not oil, gas, minerals or equipment) from a bank, government or other regular lender'. In the help, add 'Yes for a nonrecourse loan on equipment, vehicles, or oil, gas or mineral interests, even from a bank.'

findings.who: A filer who bought into a syndicated rental property with a nonrecourse mortgage. The lender is affiliated with the promoter or broker, who earned a fee from the filer's investment. The lender is otherwise a regular commercial lender.
findings.why_no: The help lists the seller, a co-owner, a relative of either, or a company one of them controls as reasons to say Yes. A lender that is a promoter or fee recipient is not on that list, so the filer treats it as a 'regular lender'.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3, Qualified person: 'A qualified person cannot be: ... • A person who receives a fee due to your investment in real property (or a person related to that person).'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Yes also if the lender, or someone related to it, was paid a fee for arranging or promoting your investment (for example, a syndicator, promoter or broker).'

findings.who: Married filing jointly; the spouse contributed money to a jointly held rental property. The spouse's contribution is protected by a stop-loss agreement, or the spouse borrowed it from a co-owner.
findings.why_no: The question asks about 'any money you put in'. The filer answering reads 'you' as themselves only and answers no about the spouse's contribution.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: 'Cash, property, or borrowed amounts used in the activity ... that are protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement'; 'Amounts borrowed for use in the activity from a person who has an interest in the activity'
findings.fix: Reword as 'Is any money you or your spouse put in, or any debt on it, ...'

locators: p. 3, At-Risk Rules, "In most cases, you are not at risk for amounts such as the following", and Qualified nonrecourse financing
p. 7, Line 21
p. 7, Line 21, "If you have amounts for which you are not at risk, use Form 6198 to determine the amount of your deductible loss"

findings.who: A landlord whose property manager collects the rent, keeps its fee, and sends the rest. Their year-end owner statement or Form 1099-MISC shows only the net amount.
findings.why_no: They never wrote a check for management fees, so the gate 'Management fees' feels like it does not apply. The fee was netted out of rent they never saw, and they report the net deposit as rent.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents' commissions...'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you or anyone acting for you (a property manager, rental agency, or booking platform) charge a fee to manage, rent out, or collect rent for this property, including fees taken out of rent before it reached you?' Also tell the filer to report gross rent with the fee as an expense.

findings.who: A short-term rental host who pays a booking platform host-service fee, or a co-host or leasing agent a percentage or a finder's fee, with no formal 'property management company'.
findings.why_no: They read 'management fees' as fees to a property management firm and do not see platform service fees, co-host percentages, or leasing commissions as management.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: '...management fees, agents' commissions, and depreciation.'
findings.fix: List examples in the gate's help: property manager or co-host fees, rental agency or leasing commissions, booking-platform host service fees, and rent-collection fees. Say whether commissions belong here or on line 7/19, and ask broadly before classifying.

findings.who: An owner of a royalty property, such as oil and gas interests or a copyright administered by a publisher or rights agency, who pays an administration or management fee charged against the royalties.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'For this rental property', and their property is a royalty interest, not a rental. They answer no or treat the question as inapplicable.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column... management fees'
findings.fix: Word the gate as 'For this rental or royalty property', and mention administration fees deducted from royalty payments.

findings.who: Married filers filing jointly who co-own a rental, where the spouse hired and paid the manager from the spouse's own account.
findings.why_no: The question reads as 'you'. The filer did not pay management fees personally, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column.'
findings.fix: Say 'Did you, your spouse, or any co-owner pay or owe management fees for this property?'

findings.who: Any filer reading the gate as printed.
findings.why_no: The gate text 'For this rental property — Management fees' is a label, not a question. It does not say whether a yes means 'paid', 'owed', 'billed', or 'had a manager', and it gives no year. A filer who paid in early 2025 for 2024 services, or who uses the accrual method, can answer no by reading it narrowly.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... management fees'
findings.fix: Phrase the gate as a full question: 'In 2025, did you pay (or, if you use the accrual method, incur) any fees for managing this property, including fees for earlier periods?'

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A filer whose vacation home or second home was rented part of 2025 and used personally the rest of the year. They itemize and have always deducted all of its mortgage interest on Schedule A.
findings.why_no: They read 'Mortgage interest paid to banks, etc.' for 'this rental property' as their home mortgage interest, which they believe belongs on Schedule A. The gate shows no help, so the explanation that the rented days' share goes on Schedule E (shown only with the gated question) is never seen.
findings.line: rental.amt12_if_any (and rental.mortgage_excess_if_mortgage, whose refusal is skipped)
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, 'Renting out part of your home... deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part'; p. 7, 'If you have a mortgage on your rental property, enter on line 12 the amount of interest you paid for 2025 to banks or other financial institutions.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you or your spouse pay any interest in 2025 to a bank, credit union, mortgage company or other lender on a loan secured by this property, even if you also used it as a home or deduct part of the interest elsewhere?' Show the personal-use help with the gate.

findings.who: A filer whose rental building is financed by a commercial loan, a home equity line of credit or a deed-of-trust note from a bank, credit union or nonbank mortgage servicer, and who never calls it a 'mortgage'.
findings.why_no: They take 'Mortgage' and 'banks' literally: the loan is a 'commercial loan' or a 'HELOC', or the lender is a credit union or a servicer such as a mortgage company, not a bank. They do not see 'etc.' as covering it.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, 'If you have a mortgage on your rental property, enter on line 12 the amount of interest you paid for 2025 to banks or other financial institutions.'
findings.fix: Name the lenders and loan types: 'any loan secured by this property (mortgage, deed of trust, home equity loan or line, commercial real estate loan) from a bank, credit union, mortgage company or other financial institution'.

findings.who: A filer who sold the rental, paid off its mortgage or refinanced in early 2025, so the property had no mortgage at year end. Interest was paid in January through March, including any unamortized points deductible at payoff.
findings.why_no: The input is framed as 'has_mortgage', and the gate names no year. They answer for the present ('there is no mortgage on it') and not for interest paid during 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, 'enter on line 12 the amount of interest you paid for 2025 to banks or other financial institutions... Points... must be deducted over the life of the loan.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'At any time in 2025, did you or your spouse pay interest (including points) on a loan on this property, even if the loan was paid off, refinanced or the property sold during the year?'

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where the rental's loan and Form 1098 are only in the spouse's name, or the spouse made all the payments.
findings.why_no: The filer reads the gate as asking whether they personally paid mortgage interest, and answers no because the spouse paid it.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, 'If you and at least one other person (other than your spouse if you file a joint return) were liable for and paid interest on the mortgage...' The spouse's payments count as the filer's on a joint return.
findings.fix: Say 'you or your spouse' in the gate.

findings.who: A filer who sees only one monthly 'mortgage payment' to a servicer, with escrow for taxes and insurance, and never separately 'paid interest'. Or their Form 1098 shows the interest but they think of it as their rent-collection account's outflow.
findings.why_no: The gate's short label 'Mortgage interest paid' does not prompt them to look at the interest part of a combined payment. They may confuse it with the escrowed taxes and insurance they enter elsewhere.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, 'the recipient should send you a Form 1098 or similar statement... showing the total interest received from you.'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Answer yes if you made any loan payments on this property in 2025; the interest part is on Form 1098 box 1 or your lender's year-end statement.'

locators: p. 6, Lines 12 and 13
p. 7, Line 12, "If you paid more mortgage interest than is shown on your Form 1098 or similar statement"

findings.who: An owner of a rented commercial building (or a residential rental of four or more stories) who installed energy-efficient lighting, HVAC, or envelope work placed in service in 2025. The owner is claiming a section 179D deduction figured on Form 7205.
findings.why_no: The help says an improvement or anything lasting more than a year is 'Not' other: 'list it with the buildings below.' The 179D work is an improvement, so the filer truthfully answers no. The 179D deduction is also not a cost 'paid in 2025'; it is an amount figured on Form 7205 for property placed in service.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 19: 'You may be able to deduct, on line 19, part or all of the cost of energy efficient commercial building property and energy efficient building retrofit property placed in service during the tax year. For details, see section 179D, Form 7205'
findings.fix: Ask a separate gate: 'Did you (or your spouse) place in service energy-efficient building property for this rental and figure a section 179D deduction on Form 7205?' If yes, ask for the Form 7205 amount and add it to line 19. Change the help to say: 'Improvements go with the buildings below, except a section 179D deduction from Form 7205, which goes here.'

findings.who: A landlord who paid HOA or condo association dues, pest control, a property-search or listing fee, small tools or supplies, or bank fees for the rental, and who does not know the tool's list of named expense lines.
findings.why_no: The gate's words are only 'For this rental property — Other.' The filer cannot tell what 'other' is other than, so they answer no, or assume their expense fits under an earlier category they were already asked about.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 19: 'Enter on line 19 any ordinary and necessary expenses not listed on lines 5 through 18.'
findings.fix: Reword the gate: 'For this rental property, did you (or your spouse) have any ordinary and necessary rental expenses not already entered as advertising, auto and travel, cleaning and maintenance, commissions, insurance, legal and professional fees, management fees, mortgage or other interest, repairs, supplies, taxes, utilities, or depreciation? Examples: HOA or condo dues, pest control, bank fees, small tools.'

findings.who: A landlord who paid in 2024 a multi-year cost (for example, a two-year service or monitoring contract) part of which is allocable to and deductible in 2025. Also an accrual-method landlord with a 2025 expense incurred but paid in 2026.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks for costs 'paid in 2025.' The filer reads that as excluding amounts paid in another year that are deductible for 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 19: 'any ordinary and necessary expenses not listed on lines 5 through 18' (deductible for the year, not limited to amounts paid in it; compare p. 7: 'Do not deduct prepaid interest when you paid it. You can deduct it only in the year to which it is properly allocable.')
findings.fix: Ask for other costs 'deductible for 2025: paid in 2025, or for prepaid amounts the part that belongs to 2025 (or incurred in 2025 if you use the accrual method).'

locators: p. 7, Line 19

findings.who: A filer who bought the rental with seller financing, or borrowed from a relative or a private lender, and paid that lender interest in 2025. No Form 1098 was issued.
findings.why_no: The gate says only "Other interest" and does not say other than what. The filer thinks of the payment as their mortgage, not as other interest, and leaves the box unticked.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: "Specific tracing rules apply ... In general, you allocate interest on a loan the same way you allocate the loan proceeds." Line 12 is the Form 1098 mortgage line, so mortgage interest with no Form 1098 belongs on line 13.
findings.fix: Ask: "Did you pay interest in 2025 on any loan for this property that is not shown on a Form 1098 in your name? Include a loan from the seller, a relative or another person, or a mortgage with no Form 1098."

findings.who: Co-owners, such as an unmarried couple or siblings, who are both liable on the rental mortgage. The Form 1098 lists only the other owner, and this filer paid their share of the interest.
findings.why_no: The filer sees one mortgage with one Form 1098. They treat it as mortgage interest, not other interest, and may think it belongs to the person named on the form.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Lines 12 and 13 (tracing and allocation of interest). The gated question itself shows the IRS rule: "a loan with no Form 1098 in your name."
findings.fix: In the gate, include "your share of mortgage interest where the Form 1098 is in someone else's name."

findings.who: A filer who paid for the rental or its improvements with a home equity loan or cash-out refinance on their main home or another property, or with a personal loan, a credit card, or a margin loan.
findings.why_no: The gate is asked "For this rental property." The loan is secured by a different property, or by no property, so the filer decides the interest belongs to that other loan and not to this rental.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: "you allocate interest on a loan the same way you allocate the loan proceeds. You allocate loan proceeds by tracing disbursements to specific uses."
findings.fix: Ask: "Was any money you borrowed spent on this property, whatever secured the loan (your home, another property, a credit card, a margin account, a personal loan)?" Move the examples from the gated help text into the gate.

findings.who: A filer who paid points or loan fees on the rental's loan in an earlier year and deducts each year's share over the loan's life. Another case is a filer who refinanced or paid off the loan in 2025, leaving unamortized points.
findings.why_no: The filer paid no interest beyond the Form 1098 amount in 2025 and does not see points from years ago as other interest. The gated question's wording "paid in 2025" reinforces this.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Lines 12 and 13 (interest allocable to rental activities). The gated question says: "for points or loan fees, only 2025's share, spread evenly over the loan."
findings.fix: Add to the gate: "or points or loan fees paid in any year that you are spreading over the loan (including the unspread rest if the loan ended in 2025)." In the gated question, say "deductible for 2025" rather than "paid in 2025."

findings.who: A filer who uses a financed car partly for the rental (driving to repairs and showings) and deducts actual auto expenses.
findings.why_no: The filer treats car loan interest as a vehicle expense covered under auto and travel, not as interest on this rental.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 6: "If you ... claimed a deduction in 2025 on Schedule 1-A ... for the vehicle loan interest allocable to your personal use, then you can't claim a deduction for that same interest on Schedule E." This implies the rental-use share is deductible on Schedule E.
findings.fix: List "the rental share of interest on a car loan, if you use actual auto expenses" among the gate's examples.

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse alone took out a personal or home equity loan and spent the money on the couple's rental.
findings.why_no: The filer did not borrow anything and is not liable on the loan, so they answer no for the property.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: "you allocate interest on a loan the same way you allocate the loan proceeds."
findings.fix: Ask: "Did you or your spouse pay interest on money borrowed and spent on this property ..."

locators: p. 6, Lines 12 and 13

findings.who: A landlord who repainted a unit between tenants, re-caulked tubs and serviced the furnace in 2025. Nothing was broken.
findings.why_no: The gate's only word is 'Repairs'. Repainting and routine servicing are upkeep, not fixing something broken, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 14: 'You can deduct the amounts paid for repairs and maintenance... Examples are fixing a broken lock or painting a room.'
findings.fix: Word the gate as 'Did you pay for repairs or maintenance that keep this property in working order in 2025 (for example, fixing a broken lock or painting a room)?'

findings.who: A landlord who files on a cash basis. A contractor fixed a leak in December 2024, and the landlord paid the invoice in January 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate names no year. The filer thinks of work done during 2025, finds none, and answers no, even though the gated question counts repairs paid in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 14: 'You can deduct the amounts paid for repairs and maintenance.'
findings.fix: State the time frame by payment date: 'Did you pay for any repairs or maintenance on this property in 2025, even for work done earlier?'

findings.who: A landlord whose tenant paid a plumber for a repair and deducted the cost from rent, or a landlord whose spouse paid the repair bill on a jointly owned property on a joint return.
findings.why_no: The filer reads the gate, and the gated question's 'paid... (your share)', as asking what the filer personally paid. Because someone else paid, the filer answers no. The tenant-paid amount is rental income and a deductible repair; the spouse's payment counts on a joint return.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 14: 'You can deduct the amounts paid for repairs and maintenance.' (The rule for tenant-paid expenses is in Pub. 527, which is not in this excerpt.)
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you, your spouse, or a tenant on your behalf (in place of rent) pay for repairs or maintenance on this property in 2025?' Make sure the tenant-paid amount also reaches rents received.

findings.who: Any landlord who sees the bare label 'For this rental property — Repairs' as a yes/no gate.
findings.why_no: The label does not ask a question. A filer may read it as 'does the property need repairs?' or as a section heading, answer no, and skip it.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 14: 'You can deduct the amounts paid for repairs and maintenance.'
findings.fix: Phrase the gate as a full question about amounts paid in 2025, and show the repair-versus-improvement help at the gate as well as at the gated question.

findings.who: A landlord who patched a leaking section of roof or replaced a broken furnace igniter in 2025.
findings.why_no: The help names 'a new roof, a new furnace' as improvements. If the filer has seen that help, or believes anything touching the roof or furnace is an improvement, the filer answers no to repairs.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 14: 'Repairs and maintenance costs are those costs that keep the property in an ordinarily efficient operating condition.'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Fixing part of a roof, furnace or other system so it keeps working is a repair. Replacing the whole system is an improvement.'

locators: p. 7, Line 14

findings.who: A landlord who bought cleaning products, light bulbs, smoke-detector batteries, filters and small hardware for the rental during 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate is the single word "Supplies" with no examples. The filer thinks of these purchases as cleaning, upkeep or repairs, not "supplies", and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: "You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance..."
findings.fix: Ask: "In 2025, did you or anyone for you (spouse, manager, tenant) buy any items used up in running this rental, such as cleaning products, light bulbs, batteries, filters, small hardware or office supplies?" Then ask for the amount.

findings.who: A filer who rents out a room or one unit of the home they live in and buys household supplies used in both the rented and the personal part.
findings.why_no: The filer sees the purchases as ordinary household shopping, not rental supplies, so answers no. The help never says that shared supplies are entered before the split.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part."
findings.fix: Add to the gate: "Include supplies shared with your own living space; we will apply the rented-part share later."

findings.who: An owner whose property manager bought supplies and subtracted them from the rent paid to the owner, or whose tenant bought supplies and took them off the rent.
findings.why_no: The filer never paid for supplies directly. They read the question as asking about their own purchases, or they report only the net rent they received.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property... You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... management fees"
findings.fix: Say in the gate: "including supplies bought by a property manager or tenant and taken out of the rent." Also make sure gross rent is reported before those amounts are taken out.

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse co-owns the rental and bought all of its supplies in 2025.
findings.why_no: The amount question says "your share". The person entering the return bought nothing themselves, so they answer no or enter only half.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column."
findings.fix: Say "supplies bought by you or your spouse for this property". On a joint return, define the share as the combined share of both spouses.

findings.who: An owner of a royalty property, such as a mineral interest or copyright, who paid for supplies used in that activity.
findings.why_no: The gate says "For this rental property". A royalty owner does not see their property as a rental and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column."
findings.fix: Say "For this rental or royalty property".

findings.who: A filer who bought supplies in late 2025 on credit or on account and paid for them in 2026, or who paid in 2025 for supplies received or used in 2026.
findings.why_no: The gate states no year, but the amount says "paid in 2025". Filers are unsure which year counts and may answer no or use the wrong year.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property" (the same page uses "paid or incurred in 2025" for other expenses)
findings.fix: State the timing rule in the gate: "supplies paid for in 2025 (a credit-card charge counts as paid when charged)".

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A filer with an oil, gas or mineral royalty property listed on Schedule E. The producer withheld state severance or production taxes from the royalty checks, and line 4 is reported gross as instructed.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'For this rental property — Taxes', and the gated question asks for 'Property tax and other taxes on it, paid in 2025'. A royalty interest is not a rental property, and the filer never paid the tax; the producer withheld it. So the truthful answer is no, or the filer enters nothing.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 4: 'Enter on line 4 the gross amount of royalty income, even if state or local taxes were withheld from oil or gas payments you received. Include taxes withheld by the producer on line 16.'
findings.fix: Word the gate as 'For this rental or royalty property — did you or your spouse pay any taxes on it in 2025, or did a producer or payer withhold any taxes (such as severance or production tax) from your royalty payments?' Add a separate gated input for producer-withheld taxes on royalty properties, and add it to line 16.

findings.who: An owner whose property tax on the rental is paid from a mortgage escrow account by the lender or servicer, and reported on Form 1098.
findings.why_no: The owner never writes a tax check ('paid', 'Taxes') and thinks of the payment as part of the mortgage, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, ...'
findings.fix: Add to the gate help: 'Include property tax paid for you from a mortgage escrow account (often shown on Form 1098) and real estate taxes you were treated as paying at closing.'

findings.who: A filer who rents out a room or one unit of the home (or duplex) they live in, and pays one property tax bill for the whole building.
findings.why_no: The tax bill is on their home and they deduct it on Schedule A, so 'Taxes' for 'this rental property' reads as no. The help covers only a day-based split for a home that was also used personally; it never mentions splitting by the part of the home that is rented.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Renting out part of your home. If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part.'
findings.fix: Gate help: 'If you rent out only part of your home or building, answer yes when the property has a tax bill, and enter the part of the tax that applies to the rented part (for example, by area). The rest goes with your home's property tax.'

findings.who: A cooperative-housing tenant-stockholder who rents out their co-op unit and pays the property's real estate tax through monthly maintenance charges.
findings.why_no: They pay 'maintenance', not a tax bill, so 'Taxes' and 'Property tax ... on it' read as no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, ...'
findings.fix: Gate help: 'For a co-op unit, include your share of the corporation's real estate taxes paid through maintenance charges (shown on the co-op's statement).'

findings.who: A short-term rental owner who pays the employer's share of payroll taxes for a cleaner or manager, a local rental business-license tax, or a lodging tax that is levied on the owner.
findings.why_no: The gated question says 'Property tax and other taxes on it', and these taxes are not 'on' the property. The filer reads the line as property tax only and answers no, or omits these amounts.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, ...'
findings.fix: Word the gate as 'Did you or your spouse pay any taxes for this rental in 2025 (property tax, or taxes of the rental activity such as payroll taxes for its workers or license and occupancy taxes you owe)?'

findings.who: Joint filers who co-own a rental, where the spouse paid the property tax from a separate account.
findings.why_no: The question says 'your share' and gives no 'you or your spouse', so the filer who did not pay answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column. You can deduct ... taxes'
findings.fix: Say 'you or your spouse (on a joint return)' in both the gate and the amount question.

locators: p. 6, Line 16

findings.who: A landlord whose tenants pay all the electric, gas and water bills directly. The landlord's only line-17 cost is long-distance or cell-phone calls to the renter, or a separate second phone line used for the rental.
findings.why_no: The gate says only "Utilities". Most filers read that as power, gas, water and trash, not telephone calls, so they truthfully answer no about those services.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 7, Line 17: "You can deduct the cost of ordinary and necessary telephone calls related to your rental activities or royalty income (for example, calls to the renter)."
findings.fix: Ask: "Did you or a tenant (in place of rent) pay utilities for this property (electricity, gas, water, sewer, trash, heating fuel), or telephone, cell-phone or internet costs for your rental activity, such as calls to the renter?" State in help that the base rate of the first phone line into your home is excluded.

findings.who: A filer who reports only royalty income on Schedule E, such as mineral or book royalties, and pays for telephone calls related to that royalty income.
findings.why_no: The gate opens with "For this rental property". A royalty owner has no rental property and answers no, or never reaches the gate.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 7, Line 17: "telephone calls related to your rental activities or royalty income"
findings.fix: Word the gate "For this rental or royalty property". Confirm that royalty properties reach this gate and are not excluded by a parent question about rental property.

findings.who: A landlord whose tenant paid the property's water or electric bill and deducted it from the rent, or paid it instead of rent.
findings.why_no: The gate says only "Utilities" and does not mention tenant payments. The landlord paid no utility bill and answers no, though the gated question itself counts "by a tenant in place of rent".
findings.irs_text: The gated input rental.amt17, citing i1040se p. 7, Line 17: "Utilities for it, paid in 2025 by you or by a tenant in place of rent (your share)". Page 7 itself does not state the tenant-payment rule.
findings.fix: Add to the gate: "including any utility bills a tenant paid for you in place of rent". Also make sure those amounts are included in rents received.

findings.who: The owner of a vacation home that they also used personally. The owner paid all the utilities and assumes they are personal because the owner lived there part of the year.
findings.why_no: The gate asks "For this rental property — Utilities" and gives no hint that a shared or partly personal expense counts before it is divided. The owner answers no, expecting nothing to be deductible.
findings.irs_text: The tool's own help for the gated line: "Utilities paid in 2025, before any division for personal use". The cited i1040se p. 7, Line 17 text does not address this split.
findings.fix: Add help text to the gate: "Answer yes even if you also used the property personally; the tool divides the cost later."

locators: p. 7, Line 17

findings.who: A filer rents out bare land and picks property type 'land' on line 1b. The rental has net passive income for the year, including a gain from selling the land.
findings.why_no: The tool computes rental.is_land as true, so it never asks the 30% question and sets land_heavy_if_built to false. Nothing in the gate shows another line applying the nondepreciable-property rule for land-only rentals. Land with nothing depreciable has 0% depreciable basis, which is under 30%.
findings.irs_text: p925 (2025) p. 16: "less than 30% of the unadjusted basis of the property is subject to depreciation, you treat the net passive income as nonpassive income."
findings.fix: Set the line to true when rental.is_land is true. Or define the downstream test as (rental.is_land OR rental.land_heavy_if_built) and name the line so it is clear it covers only built property.

findings.who: A filer inherited, was given, or got by like-kind exchange a lot with a small building or fixtures on it, and now rents it out.
findings.why_no: The question asks about 'what it cost', and the help says 'what you paid'. The filer paid nothing, or paid with other property, so they answer no or cannot apply the split. The test uses unadjusted basis, which here is the value at death, the donor's carryover basis, or the exchanged basis, not a purchase price.
findings.irs_text: p925 (2025) p. 16: "less than 30% of the unadjusted basis of the property is subject to depreciation"
findings.fix: Ask: 'Of your starting basis in this property (what you paid, or its value or basis if you inherited it, received it as a gift, or got it in an exchange, before any depreciation), was less than 30% for buildings, improvements, and other things that wear out?'

findings.who: A filer whose land rental shows a loss from operations, but who sold the property this year at a gain, or has prior-year unallowed losses that the current income absorbs.
findings.why_no: The help says a Yes matters 'only if it makes money'. The filer reads 'makes money' as rent minus expenses, decides a Yes is irrelevant, and answers no without checking the split. Under Pub 925, net passive income includes the disposition gain, and it is measured together with prior-year unallowed losses.
findings.irs_text: p925 (2025) p. 16, Example: "Charlie's net passive income from the activity (which is figured with the gain from the disposition, including gain from the improvements) is treated as nonpassive income."
findings.fix: Drop the outcome hint from the help, or say: 'answer from the cost split alone; whether it matters (including any gain on selling the property this year) is figured later.'

findings.who: A filer rents land that has a small fence, well, or paving, and picks line 1b 'land' because the property is mostly land.
findings.why_no: The gate's label, 'nothing on it subject to depreciation', does not match the facts. The 30% question is skipped, and the tool may treat the property as having no depreciable basis at all. The 30% result is still right in most such cases, but depreciation on the improvements may be dropped.
findings.irs_text: p925 (2025) p. 16: "The unadjusted basis of the improvements ($100,000) equals 25% of the unadjusted basis of all property ($400,000) used in the rental activity."
findings.fix: When line 1b is 'land', confirm: 'Is there anything on the land you paid for that wears out, such as a fence, well, paving, or shed?' If yes, ask the 30% question.

locators: p. 16, Rental of Nondepreciable Property, "less than 30% of the unadjusted basis of the property is subject to depreciation"

findings.who: A joint filer who does not personally manage the rental, but whose spouse actively participates in the current year; the rental has a prior-year unallowed loss, part of which arose in a year when neither spouse actively participated.
findings.why_no: The gate/helper is labeled only 'Active participation' and the filer reads it as asking about the filer's own participation. They truthfully answer no for themselves even though the spouse's participation makes the joint return active; the gate then skips the prior-year question.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 4: 'You aren’t considered to actively participate in a rental real estate activity if at any time during the tax year your interest (including your spouse's interest) in the activity was less than 10%'; i8582 p. 10: 'Don’t enter a prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part IV unless you actively participated in the activity in both the year the loss arose and the current tax year.'
findings.fix: Make the gate and helper explicitly per return, e.g. 'Did you or your spouse actively participate in the current tax year?', and ask the prior-year question with the same spouse-inclusive wording.

findings.who: A filer who did not make management decisions in the current year but did arrange repairs or other services in a significant and bona fide sense; the rental has a held-back loss, part of which came from a prior year without active participation.
findings.why_no: The gate asks for the legal conclusion 'Active participation', and the gated question’s wording focuses on 'helped make its decisions'. The filer answers no because they did not make decisions, missing that arranging services can count.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 4: 'You may be treated as actively participating if, for example, you participated in making management decisions or arranged for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense.'
findings.fix: Ask facts rather than the conclusion, and include both management decisions and arranging services in the gate/help; or treat either as active participation before asking the prior-year question.

findings.who: A filer who actively participated in 2025 but did not actively participate in the earlier year in which the held-back loss arose; the 2024 return shows a prior-year unallowed loss for the rental.
findings.why_no: The gate/helper says only 'Active participation' without saying 'current tax year'. The filer reads it as active participation in both the year the loss arose and the current year, so answers no because they were not active when the loss arose.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10: 'Don’t enter a prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part IV unless you actively participated in the activity in both the year the loss arose and the current tax year. If you didn’t actively participate in both years, enter the prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part V.'
findings.fix: State 'in the current tax year' in the gate/helper, and let the gated question capture the prior-year fact; do not fold both years into the gate.

findings.who: A filer whose 2024 Form 8582, Part VII, column (c) shows a prior-year unallowed loss for the rental, but who does not recognize the phrase 'held back' as referring to that carryover.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'a loss from this rental [was] held back on the 2024 return'. The filer thinks no because they did not use that label and may not know Form 8582 Part VII column (c) is the carried-over unallowed loss.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10: 'Column (c). Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582.'
findings.fix: Ask a checkable fact: 'Did your 2024 Form 8582, Part VII, column (c) show an unallowed loss for this rental?' and only then ask whether any part came from a non-active year.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "Don’t enter a prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part IV unless you actively participated in the activity in both the year the loss arose and the current tax year"
p. 4, Part IV

findings.who: A filer whose rental loss in an earlier year was partly allowed under the $25,000 special allowance and partly carried forward, because of income phase-out or because losses exceeded $25,000. Their earlier return showed a rental loss deduction.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'a loss from this rental [was] held back (not deducted)'. The filer remembers deducting the loss and reads the question as asking whether the whole loss was disallowed. They answer no and drop the unallowed remainder.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV, Column (c): "Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.fix: Ask: 'Was any part of a loss from this rental not deducted (carried forward) on an earlier return, even if some of the loss was deducted?'

findings.who: A filer who used a vacation unit personally in an earlier year and rented it 15 days or more. Worksheet 5-1 limited the expenses, so Schedule E showed zero net income and no loss, and there was no Form 8582.
findings.why_no: The help says 'Look for Form 8582 in your 2024 return' and 'Answer No if none of your rentals had a loss before 2025.' The filer finds no Form 8582 and sees no loss on Schedule E, because the excess expenses were held off it. They answer no despite the 'Yes also' sentence, and the interview never reaches the refusal.
findings.irs_text: p527 (2025) p. 28: "The excess expenses that can't be used to offset income from other sources are carried forward to the next year and treated as rental expenses for the same property ... This limitation will apply to expenses carried forward to another year even if you don't use the property as your home for that subsequent year."
findings.fix: Remove 'Answer No if none of your rentals had a loss' or qualify it. State in the gate itself: 'or were rental expenses for this property carried to a later year on Pub. 527 Worksheet 5-1 (a worksheet kept with your records, not a filed form), even if Schedule E showed no loss?'

findings.who: A filer whose rental was used in an earlier year by a relative, a co-owner, or a tenant paying below fair rent for more than 14 days. The filer never stayed there, and Worksheet 5-1 carried expenses forward.
findings.why_no: The help says 'Yes also for costs carried over from a year it counted as your home through personal use.' The filer never lived there, so they read 'your home' as excluding a relative's or co-owner's use. The broader definition appears only in the gated question, which a no never reaches.
findings.irs_text: p527 (2025) p. 28: "To figure your deductible rental expenses and any carryover to next year, use Worksheet 5-1." (personal use by others makes the unit 'used as a home')
findings.fix: Move the definition into the gate's help: 'personal use includes use by you, a co-owner, a relative, or anyone paying less than fair rent, even if you never stayed there.'

findings.who: A filer whose 2024 Form 8582 lists this property under a grouped or differently named activity, or who did not file a 2024 return and has an unallowed loss from 2023 or earlier.
findings.why_no: The help points only to 'Form 8582 in your 2024 return.' The filer finds no line naming this property, or has no 2024 return, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i8582 (2025) p. 10, Part IV: "Don't enter a prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part IV unless you actively participated ... enter the prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part V."
findings.fix: Add: 'If the property was part of a combined activity, or your last Form 8582 is from an earlier year, answer Yes if any unallowed loss is shown for it.'

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"
p. 28, "The excess expenses that can’t be used to offset income from other sources are carried forward to the next year and treated as rental expenses for the same property"
p. 28, Used as a home and rented 15 days or more

findings.who: A filer whose rental activity rents more than one class of property, for example short daily rentals that bring in most of the income alongside one low-rent long lease. Take ten 3-day rentals earning 99% of gross rental income and one 365-day lease earning 1%.
findings.why_no: The help says to divide the days rented by the number of separate stays: 395 / 11 = 35.9 days, so the honest answer is no. The IRS rule weights each class's average by its share of gross rental income: 3 x 0.99 + 365 x 0.01 = 6.6 days. That is 7 days or less.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3, Exceptions: "If the activity involves renting more than one class of property, multiply the average period of customer use of each class by the ratio of the gross rental income from that class to the activity's total gross rental income. The activity's average period of customer use equals the sum of these class-by-class average periods weighted by gross income."
findings.fix: First ask whether the activity rents more than one kind of property, such as rooms and equipment, or units with different rental terms. If yes, compute the income-weighted average from per-class days, stays and gross rent. Do not use a single days-per-stay division.

findings.who: A vacation rental owner who listed the property all year (365 days) and had 10 bookings of about 4 nights each.
findings.why_no: "Days it was rented" can be read as the days the property was rented out or offered for rent, not the nights renters actually occupied it. Then 365 / 10 = 36.5 days, more than 30, so the filer answers no. The true average is about 4 days.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3, Exceptions: "dividing the total number of days in all rental periods by the number of rentals during the tax year"; exception 1a: "The average period of customer use is: a. 7 days or less"
findings.fix: Say: "Add up only the days renters actually had use of it. Do not count days it was listed or vacant, or days you used it yourself. Divide by the number of separate rentals."

findings.who: An owner whose property is booked repeatedly by the same renters, for example a corporate client that took 12 separate 5-day stays and a family that came back four times for a week.
findings.why_no: "Number of separate stays" can be read as the number of renters or customers. Counting each repeat client once shrinks the divisor and pushes the average above 30 days, or at least above 7.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3, Exceptions: "dividing the total number of days in all rental periods by the number of rentals during the tax year"
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Count each rental period (booking) separately, even when the same renter comes back."

findings.who: An owner who switched in 2025 from short-term stays to a long lease, or the reverse, and also counts days in a lease or booking that started in 2024 or runs into 2026.
findings.why_no: The question has no tax-year limit, and the help example of "a one-year lease is one stay of 365 days" invites counting a whole lease that crosses years. That can raise the average above 30 even though the 2025 rental periods average 7 days or less.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3, Exceptions: "by the number of rentals during the tax year"
findings.fix: Add "in 2025" to the question and state how to count rental periods that cross the start or end of the year.

locators: p. 3, Exceptions
p. 3, Exceptions, "Figure the average period of customer use for a class of property by dividing the total number of days in all rental periods by the number of rentals"
